scenes.caption: Same amount of money on both sides. But losing ₹10,000 usually weighs more than gaining ₹10,000.
When prices drop, the paper loss starts to feel intolerable — even if your reason for investing hasn't changed.
Selling then is driven by the discomfort of watching the number fall, not by new evidence.
Write down why you bought, your time horizon, and when you would sell — before the next fall.
A step that is right 95% of the time sounds excellent.
Chain the steps and the odds multiply: ten 95% steps succeed end to end about 60% of the time.
Over ten steps: 99% per step gives about 90%; 90% per step gives about 35%.
Long agent chains need fewer steps, checks between them, or both.
A weekly one-on-one is the one slot that belongs to the report, not to the manager's agenda.
Status can live in tickets. Use the time for blockers, career direction, feedback both ways — and what's draining them.
Keep it regular and rarely cancel it — each cancellation tells them where they rank.
A simple test of quality: who spoke for most of the time?
Returns start earning returns of their own. Growth builds on a growing base, so the curve looks flat for years and steep later.
Illustration only, at a constant 8%: ₹1,00,000 becomes about ₹2,00,000 after nine years and about ₹4,00,000 after eighteen.
The second doubling adds twice as much money as the first, for the same nine years of waiting. Real returns are not constant.
A rough rule of thumb for doubling time: divide 72 by the annual rate. At 8% a year, that is roughly nine years.
Costs and taxes compound too, and inflation shrinks what the final amount can buy. The power is in time, not one clever move.
Two portfolios can earn the same average annual return and still end in very different places if money is being taken out.
Illustration only, not a forecast: ₹1 crore, ₹6 lakh withdrawn yearly. Weak years first mean selling more units at low prices.
The same returns in reverse order leave you better off, because more was left to recover before the losses arrived.
While you only contribute, order matters little. Once you withdraw, the timing of losses becomes a central risk.
If your money earns 7% before tax but prices rise 5%, your real gain is closer to 2%.
Illustration only: ₹1,00,000 at 6% becomes ₹1,06,000. If prices also rose 6%, the same basket costs about ₹1,06,000 too.
Real return is roughly the rate you earn minus inflation, and less after tax. In some years it can be negative.
Cash that feels safe can quietly lose purchasing power. Safe assets aren't bad — but you should be able to name the price.
Illustration only: you start at 60% equity. After a strong year for equities you are at 70%, so a fall now hurts more.
Leaving winners alone feels pleasant. The result is a risk level set by the market, not by you.
Rebalancing brings the mix back to target: sell some of what grew, buy what lagged, or direct new money to the lagging part.
Pick a rule — say once a year, or when the split drifts by more than five points — and let the plan decide, not your mood.
'Sort out the escalation backlog.' The lead wanted a triage proposal; the engineer closed twenty tickets.
Name the level: look into it, recommend, decide but tell me first, act then inform, or fully own it.
The task can stay the same while the level moves up as trust and skill grow.
When you hand something off, finish with: 'For this one, you're at level __.'
Your BATNA is what you will do if this negotiation fails. Compare every offer with it, not with your hopes.
Illustrative: another vendor quotes ₹16 lakh, plus ₹1.5 lakh in switching costs. Your BATNA is ₹17.5 lakh all-in.
The current vendor wants ₹18 lakh to renew. Any renewal offer below ₹17.5 lakh is better than walking away.
Write your BATNA in one line, work on improving it, and estimate theirs. Don't bluff about it.
Busy readers decide in the first two lines whether to keep reading. Most messages bury the ask in the last paragraph.
Lead with the answer, support it with a few grouped reasons, and put the detail beneath.
Illustrative: approval needed by Thursday for two temporary agents. Then the reasons. Then 'detail below'.
For hard news, a short lead-in may land better. And if you can't state the answer in a sentence, the thinking is unfinished.
A language model splits your text into small pieces called tokens — whole words or word fragments.
It ranks possible next tokens by how plausible they are in context — like 'off', 'blinking' or 'green'. Sizes here are schematic.
It picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats — one small piece at a time.
There is no fact table lookup at that moment. Answers come from learned patterns, shaped by the words you supply.
Add 'The customer says' or paste the device manual, and the ranking shifts. That's why supplied documents matter so much.
A model can only consider what's inside its context window: your instructions, pasted documents and the conversation so far.
In studies of long inputs, models often used information near the start or end better than information buried in the middle.
Position effects vary by model and task, and newer models may show them less. Test on your own data.
Illustrative: a 60-page guide hides the key caveat on page 31 and the answer misses it. Only the relevant section gets it right.
Move the key instruction and key evidence to the start or end, and trim the rest.
Larger models tend to be slower and costlier per request. Smaller ones are quicker and cheaper but may struggle with hard reasoning.
Illustrative: tagging goes to a small model, tricky multi-device faults to a larger one, refund decisions to a person.
Test the split instead of assuming it: let the small model say 'escalate', sample its outputs, and re-check when things change.
A cheaper model for easy work is a design choice, not a compromise.
Serious incidents rarely come from one big mistake.
Each defence is a slice with holes. Illustrative: testing, release checklist, monitoring and runbook all had a gap.
Any one slice usually stops the problem. An incident happens when the holes in several layers line up. Bar sizes are schematic.

scenes.chapter: Fix more than the last hole
scenes.caption: Stop treating the last person to touch it as the cause. Strengthen many layers a little — it's a metaphor, not a measurement.
In a stable system, the average number of items inside equals arrival rate times the average time each stays.
Illustrative: 40 new escalations a day, each open for 3 days on average, means about 120 open at any time.
Cut the average stay to 2 days, for instance by removing a hand-off wait, and about 80 are open — with nobody working faster.
The question shifts from 'we need more people closing cases' to 'where are cases waiting?'
A manager's day is chopped into one-hour slots. A maker's day runs in half-day units, because deep work needs unbroken blocks.
Illustrative: a 4 pm call. Engineers wind down at 3:30 — neither half is big enough to start anything hard. Sizes are schematic.
A manager sees a thirty-minute call. The engineer loses the afternoon.
Cluster meetings, move them to the start or end of the day, or swap one for a written update. Real urgency still wins.
A queue can be ordered by arrival time, by customer importance, or by impact and urgency. Each gives a very different Monday.
Illustrative: a 40-vehicle fleet has cameras offline; a large account asks about billing. Impact and urgency put the fleet first.
Without an explicit rule, priority drifts to whoever escalates loudest, and real emergencies wait behind them.
The matrix is harder to run but forces the real question: how bad, and how soon?
In the 1993 study, one trial was 60 seconds in cold water; the other added 30 seconds in slightly warmer water.
Most chose to repeat the longer trial, despite more total discomfort.
We tend to remember an experience by its most intense moment and how it ended, not its total length. Shape is schematic.
It's a tendency, not a universal rule: effects vary across situations and studies, and duration can still matter.
Avoid a bad peak and end well: recap, thank them, and confirm what happens next.
Bezos called nearly irreversible decisions one-way doors, and changeable, reversible ones two-way doors.
One-way doors deserve slow, careful deliberation. Two-way doors can be decided quickly by a person or small group.
The failure he warned about: treating reversible decisions with the heaviness meant for irreversible ones.
Illustrative: rewording a macro reply is two-way. Switching ticketing platforms is one-way. Ask the door question first.
First-order thinking asks what happens next. Second-order thinking asks: and then what, and who reacts?
Illustrative: a lead tightens handle-time targets. Cases close faster. Agents close cases early. Customers reopen them.
The backlog dips, then returns — with a worse reputation. Shape is schematic.
You can't predict every ripple. Trace two or three steps, prefer small reversible trials, and watch for the reaction you fear.
